strings.title: Times 5 as Half of Times 10, with Decimals
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: To multiply by 5, multiply by 10 and halve. It works with decimals, and it works backwards for × 0.5 (just halve).
strings.keywords: times 10, halve, times 5, times 0.5, times 50, decimals
watchFor: Halving before multiplying and losing the decimal (0.64 × 5 = 32): ask "About how big should 0.64 × 5 be?"
Thinking × 0.5 makes bigger: ask "What's half of 36?"
Forgetting the extra × 10 for × 50: ask "Is 50 ten times 5?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is × 5 the same as × 10 then halve?" Land: 5 is half of 10. × 0.5 is just halving, and × 50 is × 100 then halve.

problems.notes: Look for: ten times bigger. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: ratio 1:4.8, 10:48
Look for: half of 48. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "half of times 10". Model: ratio 1:4.8, 10:48, 5:24

responses.tip: Halved only. Ask: is 4.8 × 5 bigger or smaller than 4.8?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 36. Ask: "What does × 0.5 mean?" Model: ratio 1:36, 0.5:18

responses.tip: Ask: is half of 36 bigger than 36?

problems.notes: Look for: 72 halved. Ask: "Same as before?" Model: ratio 1:7.2, 10:72, 5:36
Look for: 6.4 halved. Ask: "About how big should it be?" Model: ratio 1:0.64, 10:6.4, 5:3.2

responses.tip: Ask: 0.64 is less than 1. Can 5 of them be 32?

problems.notes: Look for: 186 halved. Ask: "Which way do you halve 186?" Model: ratio 1:18.6, 10:186, 5:93
Look for: × 100 then halve: 246 ÷ 2. Ask: "What about × 50?" Model: ratio 1:2.46, 100:246, 50:123

strings.connection: Week 2 · Day 1: Times 5 as Half of Times 10

strings.title: Double and Halve with Decimals
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Double one factor and halve the other: the product stays the same. Keep going until one factor is friendly, like 10 or 100. It works with decimals too.
strings.keywords: double, halve, product stays the same, friendly factor, decimals
watchFor: Doubling both factors: ask "If you double one and double the other, what happens to the product?"
Stopping too early: ask "Can you keep going to a friendlier number?"
Halving the wrong factor (halving 25): ask "Which factor is easy to halve? Which becomes friendly when doubled?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does the product stay the same?" Land: doubling one factor and halving the other is ×2 ÷2, which changes nothing. Keep going until one factor is 10 or 100.

problems.notes: Look for: 50 × 2.4 = 100 × 1.2. Ask: "Which factor should you double?" Word choice: "double one, halve the other". Model: halve 25 x 4.8 = 50 x 2.4 = 100 x 1.2

responses.tip: Halved too far. Ask: halve 4.8 twice: what do you get?

problems.notes: Look for: 7 × 8. Ask: "What happens if you double 3.5?" Model: halve 3.5 x 16 = 7 x 8
Look for: 25 × 12 = 50 × 6 = 100 × 3. Ask: "How many doubles to get to 100?" Model: halve 12.5 x 24 = 25 x 12 = 50 x 6 = 100 x 3
Look for: 0.5 × 18 = 1 × 9. Or a quarter of 36. Ask: "What fraction is 0.25?" Model: halve 0.25 x 36 = 0.5 x 18 = 1 x 9
Look for: 9 × 9. Ask: "Double 4.5?" Model: halve 4.5 x 18 = 9 x 9
Look for: 2.5 × 16 = 5 × 8 = 10 × 4. Ask: "How far can you go?" Model: halve 1.25 x 32 = 2.5 x 16 = 5 x 8 = 10 x 4

strings.title: Over and Back with Decimals
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Multiply by a friendly number just over, then take back the extra groups. 19 × 3.5 is 20 × 3.5 − 3.5. With decimal factors, check what the extra group is.
strings.keywords: over and back, friendly number, take back a group, decimals, area model
watchFor: Taking back 1 instead of one group (19 × 3.5 = 70 − 1): ask "One less group of what?"
Taking back the wrong group when the decimal is in the other factor (4.99 × 8 = 40 − 0.01): ask "How much is 0.01 × 8?"
Losing the decimal: ask "About how big should 99 × 0.7 be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What was the extra group each time?" Land: multiply by the friendly number, then take back the extra: one group of the other factor (19 × 3.5 takes back 3.5), or 0.01 of it (4.99 × 8 takes back 0.08).

problems.notes: Look for: 20 × 3.5 − 3.5 = 70 − 3.5. Ask: "What's one more group?" Word choice: "take back a group". Model: area 20-1 x 3.5

responses.tip: Took back 1, not one group of 3.5. Ask: one less group of what?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 6 − 0.1 × 6 = 18 − 0.6. Ask: "How far is 2.9 from 3?" Model: area 3-0.1 x 6

responses.tip: Took back 0.1, not 0.1 × 6. Ask: how many 0.1s did you add?

problems.notes: Look for: 100 × 0.7 − 0.7 = 70 − 0.7. Ask: "Same move?" Model: area 100-1 x 0.7
Look for: 5 × 8 − 0.01 × 8 = 40 − 0.08. Ask: "What's the extra?" Model: area 5-0.01 x 8

responses.tip: Ask: 8 of them were each 0.01 too big. How much too much?

problems.notes: Look for: 20 × 1.5 + 1.5 = 30 + 1.5. Ask: "Over or under?" Model: area 20+1 x 1.5
Look for: 25 − 0.02 × 25 = 25 − 0.5. Ask: "What's 0.98 close to?" Model: area 1-0.02 x 25
Look for: 200 × 0.3 − 0.3. Ask: "Which way?" Model: area 200-1 x 0.3

strings.title: Dividing by 5, 25 and 50
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Dividing by 5 is dividing by 10 and doubling. Dividing by 25 is dividing by 100 and multiplying by 4. Dividing by 50 is dividing by 100 and doubling.
strings.keywords: divide, times 2, times 4, divide by 10, divide by 100, how many groups
watchFor: Halving instead of doubling (120 ÷ 5 = 6): ask "Are there more 5s or more 10s in 120?"
Losing the decimal (460 ÷ 25 = 184): ask "About how many 25s in 460?"
Not seeing 90 ÷ 2.5 as 900 ÷ 25: ask "Could you multiply both by 10?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why do we double when we divide by 5?" Land: 5 is half of 10, so twice as many 5s fit as 10s. For 25, four times as many fit as 100s.

problems.notes: Look for: 12 tens, so 24 fives. Ask: "How many 10s? How many 5s?" Model: ratio 10:12, 5:24

responses.tip: Halved instead of doubling. Ask: are there more 5s or more 10s in 120?

problems.notes: Look for: 1.2 hundreds, × 4. Ask: "How many 25s in a hundred?" Model: ratio 100:1.2, 25:4.8

responses.say: 4 quarters in each dollar: $1.20 is 4.8 quarters.

problems.notes: Look for: 3.5 hundreds, doubled. Ask: "How many 50s in 100?" Model: ratio 100:3.5, 50:7
Look for: 4.6 × 4. Ask: "About how many?" Model: ratio 100:4.6, 25:18.4

responses.tip: Ask: about how many 25s fit in 460? Fewer than 20?

problems.notes: Look for: 0.75 doubled. Ask: "Same move with a decimal?" Model: ratio 10:0.75, 5:1.5
Look for: 900 ÷ 25 = 9 × 4. Ask: "Could you multiply both by 10?" Model: text 90 ÷ 2.5 = 900 ÷ 25 ; = 9 x 4 = 36

responses.say: 2.5 fits 4 times in 10, so 36 times in 90.

problems.notes: Look for: 125 × 8 = 1000. Ask: "What do you know about 125?" Model: halve 125 x 8 = 250 x 4 = 500 x 2 = 1000 x 1

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy, Round 2
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Look at the factors first: is one near a friendly number? Can you double and halve? Is there a 5 or 25? Then choose.
strings.keywords: choose, double and halve, over and back, times 5, divide by 25, friendly factor
watchFor: Using the algorithm for 4.5 × 22: ask "Can you double one and halve the other?"
Over and back with the wrong group: ask "One less group of what?"
Not estimating: ask "About how big should it be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What did you notice first?" Land: a factor near a friendly number means over and back; an even factor with a 5, 25 or decimal means double and halve; × 5 or ÷ 25 means think in 10s or 100s.

problems.notes: Look for: 9 × 11. Ask: "Double and halve?" Model: halve 4.5 x 22 = 9 x 11
Look for: 40 × 2.5 − 2.5 = 100 − 2.5. Ask: "Over and back?" Model: area 40-1 x 2.5

responses.tip: Ask: one less group of what?

problems.notes: Look for: 64 halved. Ask: "Which strategy fits these numbers?" Model: ratio 1:6.4, 10:64, 5:32
Look for: 3.4 × 4. Ask: "Which strategy fits these numbers?" Model: ratio 100:3.4, 25:13.6
Look for: half of a half. Ask: "Bigger or smaller than 0.5?" Model: area 0.5 x 0.5

responses.tip: Added. Ask: what is half of a half?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 1.2 (double and halve), or 2.4 + 1.2. Ask: "Which way?" Model: halve 1.5 x 2.4 = 3 x 1.2
Look for: 2 × 2.5 + 0.5 × 2.5 = 5 + 1.25. Ask: "Split a factor?" Model: area 2+0.5 x 2.5
